newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Summertime rules may not make living easy, say MEPs.
newsitem.headline: Summertime rules may not make living easy, say MEPs.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe's plans to abolish summertime could put France out of step with the whole of Europe, as MEPs back plans to set standard summertime dates throughout the European Union.
"I think Juppe's idea will be bad for France and bad for Europe," Spalato Bellere, the parliament's rapporteur on the issue, told Reuters on Tuesday.

For southern EU countries like Italy or France, having an extra hour of daylight in the evenings meant savings in energy and allowed museums and other services linked to the all- important tourist sector to function longer, the independent Italian MEP said.
But whether France chose to put its clocks forward in the summer or not was really its own affair.

The real problem came when EU countries changed their clocks at different times of the year because of the confusion this created with international plane and train timetables and international business connections, he said.

Until this year Britain, which is an hour behind Central European Time, switched back to wintertime a month later than most of its EU partners. This meant that for four weeks a year it was two hours out of synch.

To avoid confusion and loss of business in future, the European Parliament's tourism committee unanimously endorsed on Tuesday a European Commission proposal to apply summertime arrangements from the last Sunday in March to the last Sunday in October throughout the EU.
The full parliament is expected to back the draft directive - - COM(96)106 -- on November 28.
The aim of the proposal is to improve the functioning of the internal market and facilitate the operation of vital sectors such as transport and telecommunications.

While the directive will put an end to such inconveniences as the old two-hour time difference between Britain and Brussels during October, it cannot oblige France or any other member state which decides to ditch summertime altogether to change its clocks twice a year.
If Juppe goes ahead with his scheme, the first casualties of the gap between French and EU working hours will be people living on France's borders, the transport committee warned.
Another casualty will be the European Parliament itself, which moves lock, stock and barrel from Brussels to Strasbourg for a week every month.
